source.title: Open Problems in Data-Sharing Peer-to-Peer Systems

accepted.question_text: In a decentralized data-sharing peer-to-peer system that supports keyword queries, can one design a search mechanism that is both efficient in its use of bandwidth, processing, and storage and also comprehensive in the sense that it returns all matching results, without resorting to prohibitively expensive network-wide flooding?

evidence.quote: Hence, designing techniques for efficient, comprehensive search remains an open problem.

accepted.question_text: For ranked keyword search over a decentralized peer-to-peer document collection, how can the system collect and maintain the global statistics needed by state-of-the-art ranking functions, such as document-frequency information over the total collection, in a way that is simultaneously robust to failures, efficient in resource usage, and fully distributed?

evidence.quote: Collecting and maintaining these statistics in a robust, efficient, and distributed manner is a challenge.

accepted.question_text: How can ranked-search techniques for distributed systems be extended so that they remain effective at the much larger scales expected in peer-to-peer data-sharing systems, while still exploiting the possibility of returning only the top k results instead of the full result set?

evidence.quote: Techniques for ranked search exists for distributed systems of moderate scale (e.g., [7]), but future research must extend these techniques to support much larger systems.

accepted.question_text: Given existing peer-to-peer techniques for COUNT queries over predicates, can those methods be extended to support more expressive aggregate queries, including SUM, MAX, and MEDIAN, over decentralized data-sharing systems?

evidence.quote: Further research is needed to extend these techniques into more expressive aggregates like SUM, MAX, and MEDIAN.

accepted.question_text: Can a peer-to-peer search mechanism be built that supports a rich SQL-style query language over decentralized shared data with reasonable performance, and if so what architecture or alternative approach should be used to achieve that performance?

evidence.quote: A great deal of additional research is needed to advance current work into a search mechanism with reasonable performance, and to investigate alternative approaches to the problem.

accepted.question_text: Can one develop peer-to-peer search techniques that improve on the apparent tradeoffs among peer autonomy, search efficiency, and robustness, so that a system does not have to give up as much autonomy or resilience in order to obtain practical search performance?

evidence.quote: One important area of research is finding techniques that push beyond the current tradeoffs between efficiency, autonomy and robustness.

accepted.question_text: Is it possible to decouple search efficiency from peer autonomy in a data-sharing peer-to-peer system, so that peers retain substantial control over topology, data placement, and routing-related choices without sacrificing efficient search?

evidence.quote: Decoupling efficiency from autonomy seems to be the greatest challenge, since existing techniques almost uniformly sacrifice autonomy to achieve efficiency.

accepted.question_text: Is it possible to decouple peer autonomy from robustness in a peer-to-peer search mechanism, so that the system designer can vary autonomy independently while still preserving stable service under node failures and departures?

evidence.quote: Decoupling autonomy from robustness is also important, because it allows greater flexibility in choosing the desired properties of the mechanism.

accepted.question_text: Can a single peer-to-peer system provide fine-grained, user-controlled tuning of the tradeoff between autonomy and efficiency, so that different documents or use cases within the same deployment can choose different storage and search constraints without forcing users to move between separate systems?

evidence.quote: Another interesting area of research is providing fine-granularity tuning of the tradeoff between autonomy and efficiency within a single system.

accepted.question_text: For decentralized partial-search peer-to-peer systems, does there exist a general search technique that can guarantee, with high probability, that the tradeoff between resource cost and the chosen quality-of-service metric is optimal?

evidence.quote: Can there exist a general technique that can guarantee (with high probability) that the cost/QoS tradeoff is optimal?

accepted.question_text: How should future peer-to-peer protocols for data sharing be designed so that adversaries cannot easily construct denial-of-service attacks by exploiting loosely constrained protocol features such as unconstrained responses, routing behavior, or resource allocation rules?

evidence.quote: In the future, P2P protocols need to be designed to make it hard for adversaries to construct DoS attacks by taking advantage of loosely constrained protocol features.

accepted.question_text: Can peer-to-peer protocols be designed so that they do not introduce new amplification mechanisms or back-door communication channels that attackers can exploit to scale and coordinate denial-of-service attacks?

evidence.quote: It is important to design future P2P protocols such that they do not open up new opportunities for attackers to use as amplifiers and back-door communication channels.

accepted.question_text: What are the effects of denial-of-service attacks other than query-flood attacks across different peer-to-peer network designs, and what defenses are effective against those attacks in practice?

evidence.quote: However, more research is necessary to understand the effects of other types of DoS attacks in various P2P networks.

accepted.question_text: Can techniques inspired by fail-stop or Byzantine-failure handling be adapted so that they become acceptable for peer-to-peer systems from both the performance and security standpoints, despite high message overhead, complexity, and the lack of secure complete pairwise connectivity?

evidence.quote: Further research will be necessary to make these or similar techniques acceptable from a performance and security standpoint in a P2P context.

accepted.question_text: How can a peer-to-peer data-sharing system guarantee long-term file availability so that every stored file remains accessible regardless of which particular nodes are currently online and regardless of the file's popularity?

evidence.quote: We might like to ensure that all files stored in the system are always available regardless of which nodes in the network are currently online.

accepted.question_text: Given a user query and a set of returned documents in a peer-to-peer system, how can the system determine which returned documents are the authentic matches to that query, that is, what the authentic signature or set of authentic signatures should be for the documents satisfying the query?

evidence.quote: The problem of file authenticity, however, can be viewed as: given a query, what is (or are) the "authentic" signature(s) for the document(s) that satisfy the query?

accepted.question_text: In a voting-based peer-to-peer file-authenticity mechanism, how can the protocol prevent spoofing of votes, spoofing of nodes, and spoofing of files, while still letting distributed participants collectively determine authenticity?

evidence.quote: The key technical issues with this approach are how to prevent spoofing of votes, of nodes, and of files.

accepted.question_text: Can a peer-to-peer data-sharing system provide meaningful anonymity guarantees while also maintaining efficiency, decentralization, and the ability of peers to discover one another and locate content?

evidence.quote: We would ideally like to provide anonymity while maintaining other desirable search and security features such as efficiency, decentralization, and peer discovery.

accepted.question_text: Is there a peer-to-peer design that can support server anonymity, meaning that it is difficult to determine which nodes store a given document, while also supporting efficient search for that document without falling back to expensive broadcast-style search?

evidence.quote: Nevertheless, supporting server anonymity and efficient search concurrently remains an open issue.

accepted.question_text: How do anonymity protocols for peer-to-peer systems degrade under active attack, especially when intermediate proxy nodes may collude, and what protocol designs can better preserve anonymity in those adversarial settings?

evidence.quote: The degradation of anonymity protocols under attacks has been studied in [44], and this study suggests that further work is necessary in this area.

accepted.question_text: For enforcing rights over shared documents in peer-to-peer data-sharing systems, should access control be enforced by the peer-to-peer network itself or instead at the endpoints, and under what assumptions about key management and trust can either approach work?

evidence.quote: Further effort must go into exploring whether or not it is reasonable to have the P2P network enforce access control, or if the enforcements should take place at the endpoints of the network.

accepted.question_text: What is the feasibility of equipping peer-to-peer systems with technical mechanisms for intellectual-property management and digital-rights management, and which concrete protocol or system designs could make such management workable in decentralized data-sharing applications?

evidence.quote: If the benefits of P2P systems are to be realized, we need to explore the feasibility of and the technical approaches to instrumenting them with appropriate mechanisms to allow for the management of intellectual property.
